g.text: A rebalance protocol without a fencing token is broken
The generation ID is the detail most often missing from whiteboard versions - and without it a zombie consumer corrupts progress.
Partition count is a HARD CEILING on how far a group can scale out
Why not let two consumers share a partition? Ordering would break - two readers process nondeterministically, and there is no
way to track a single offset for two independent readers. Per-partition ordering and one-consumer-per-partition are the SAME
constraint viewed from two sides. Partitions are the knob that lets you choose the granularity of that trade.
The rebalance protocol, and where the fence goes
Why a CLIENT computes the assignment
Assignment strategy is application POLICY - range, round-robin, sticky, rack-aware, or something bespoke that
co-locates related partitions. Putting the planner in the client lets a team ship a custom assignor without
upgrading the cluster. The broker's job reduces to membership and distribution - the part that must be consistent.
The zombie consumer, and what the generation ID stops
Without the fence, that commit OVERWRITES the new owner's progress - rewinding it (reprocessing) or fast-forwarding it
(message loss). The zombie would also keep processing messages it no longer owns, duplicating the new owner's work.
During a rebalance EVERY member stops consuming, even those whose assignment does not change. A 100-consumer group stalls
entirely because one consumer restarted - and 98 of them then get the identical assignment back. During a rolling deploy you
pay it 100 times. Fixes: STICKY assignment (removes the wasted work), INCREMENTAL COOPERATIVE rebalancing (removes the stall -
members revoke only what they lose), and STATIC MEMBERSHIP (a consumer returning with the same member ID inside the session
timeout triggers no rebalance at all, turning a 100-rebalance deploy into zero).
